headline: One can of Coke holds about 35 g of sugar.
explanation: Coca-Cola lists 10.6 g of sugar per 100 ml. A 330 ml can adds up to about 35 g, more than the 25 g a day WHO suggests as an extra-healthy target for free sugars.
howTo: Find “sugars” per 100 ml on the label.
Multiply by the bottle size, then divide by 100.
Compare with WHO’s 25 g a day target.
note: Figures are Coca-Cola’s published values for Original Taste. Check your own bottle’s label; recipes and sizes can vary by country.

sources.title: How much sugar is in Coca-Cola Original Taste?
WHO calls on countries to reduce sugars intake among adults and children

headline: Your noodle packet hides a salt number.
explanation: Labels usually list sodium, not salt. Multiply sodium by 2.5 to get salt. WHO advises adults to keep under 2,000 mg of sodium a day, which is under 5 g of salt.
howTo: Find “sodium” on your Wai Wai or noodle packet.
Check if it’s per serving or per pack.
Sodium (mg) × 2.5 = salt (mg). Compare with 5,000 mg a day.
note: We don’t show a sodium figure for Wai Wai because we couldn’t verify one from an official label. Use the number printed on your packet.

headline: One packet isn’t always one serving.
explanation: The numbers on the back are often for a single serving, and a packet can hold more than one. Eat two servings and everything on the label doubles.
howTo: Look for “servings per pack” near the top.
Multiply any number by the servings you’ll eat.
A serving size is not a recommendation.

sources.title: How to Understand and Use the Nutrition Facts Label

headline: Apple juice keeps the sugar but loses the fibre.
explanation: A raw apple with skin has 2.4 g of fibre per 100 g. Unsweetened apple juice has 0.2 g. WHO also counts the sugar in juice as free sugar, but not the sugar in whole fruit.
howTo: Prefer the whole fruit when you can.
On juice labels, check total sugars per glass.

headline: “Wheat flour” on bread can mean white flour.
explanation: Refining removes the bran and germ, and with them virtually all the fibre. For whole grain, the first ingredient should start with “whole”, as in “whole wheat flour”.
howTo: Read the first ingredient on the bread bag.
Look for the word “whole” before the grain.
“Multigrain” alone doesn’t mean whole grain.

headline: “Made with fruit” can still mean free sugar.
explanation: WHO counts sugar from fruit juice and juice concentrate as free sugar, the same group as added table sugar. So a drink sweetened with “apple concentrate” isn’t sugar-free.
howTo: Scan the ingredients for sugar, syrup or “concentrate”.
Check total sugars per serving.
Water or plain milk have no free sugars.

headline: “Fragrance” can be a whole recipe in one word.
explanation: In the US, makers can list scent ingredients simply as “Fragrance”, because the mix counts as a trade secret. If you react to scents, that one word is worth noticing.
howTo: Look for “fragrance”, “parfum” or “perfume” in the list.
Prefer “fragrance-free” if scents bother your skin.
Patch-test new products on a small area first.
note: This describes US labelling rules. Rules in Nepal and other countries can differ.

headline: “Hypoallergenic” means whatever the brand wants.
explanation: The FDA says there’s no federal standard or definition for “hypoallergenic”, and companies don’t have to prove the claim. It’s a marketing word, not a test result.
howTo: Ignore the badge, read the ingredient list.
Check for anything you already know you react to.
note: This describes US rules. Rules in Nepal and other countries can differ.

headline: Some hair smoothing treatments release formaldehyde when heated.
explanation: The FDA warns that some smoothing and straightening products release formaldehyde gas when the hair is heated. On the label it can hide as “formalin” or “methylene glycol”.
howTo: Look for formaldehyde, formalin or methylene glycol.
Ask your salon what’s in the treatment.
Good airflow matters if it’s used.

sources.title: Hair Smoothing Products That Release Formaldehyde When Heated

headline: Supplements don’t need approval before they hit the shelf.
explanation: By law, the US FDA does not approve dietary supplements or their labels before they’re sold. Makers are responsible for safety; the FDA mostly steps in afterwards.
howTo: Treat big health claims with suspicion.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist what you take.
Check the dose against the label’s serving.
note: This describes US rules. Rules in Nepal and other countries can differ.

sources.title: Questions and Answers on Dietary Supplements
